SUMTER, June 17.—Without excitement and any appreciable display of functional political feeling the state campaign for state officers opened here today when almost two score candidates for various offices addressed about seven hundred people.

The addresses of candidates for governor contained nothing more than simple statements of the speakers' platforms. Practically all the aspirants left here tonight, for Manning where they speak tomorrow.

The Sumter court house was filled when Senator J. F. Clifton called the meeting to order at 11 o'clock. Increased attendance forced the meeting to the court house yard, where little later the noise forced them again to the court house room where the meeting was continued early in the forenoon. The candidates, numbering nearly two score, met and determined the order of speaking and time allotments. They provided that candidates for governor should speak last. Candidates for lieutenant governor followed in order by aspirants for attorney general, comptroller, adjutant general, railroad commissioners and unopposed candidates for election.

Andrew J. Bethea, of Columbia, opposed Hamer, of Dillon, and B. Frank Keil, of Bishopville, candidates for lieutenant governor; and comptroller general A. M. Stone, opposed by S. M. Smith, of Columbia; State treasurer S. A. Safford; and Secretary S. D. J. Watson, confirmed as unopposed candidates, smiled successfully.

A. G. Brice, of Chester, opposed Thos. F. Peoples, for attorney General. Candidates for railroad commissioners were led by George W. Airey, of Calhoun county and followed by C. D. Farmer, of Spartanburg, Frank W. Shealey, of Lexington, John H. Wharton of Laurens, W. L. Witherspoon of York and James Causler of Turkle. Capt. N. C. Willis, of York, candidate for adjutant General, opposed adjutant General W. W. Moore, of Barnwell.

Cheered Manning.

Deafening cheers greeted Richard I. Manning of this city, when the first gubernatorial candidate to speak came to the stand. He did not speak on the campaign issues, but stressed the necessity of law enforcement, and urged his fellow campaigners to lay aside personalities, abuse and vituperation in their addresses, as he declared for rural credit system, long term loans to tenants to make possible them owning their homes and urged educational advancement.

When Mr. Browning had concluded his address the meeting adjourned for dinner.

When the meeting convened after the dinner recess, John G. Clinkscales, of Spartanburg began speaking and stated that he was making the race for governor on his own volition, and NOT on anybody's coat tails. "If I am elected governor, I will throw every ounce of my power into redeeming my state so that we'll not be laughing stock of the people," said Professor Clinkscales. He deplored the prevalence of "pistol toting" and said men guilty of this crime should wear stripes. He advocated reform of it, etc., and the punishment of the "blind tigers."

Cooper, of Laurens, stated that he was asking tremendous responsibility but felt he was capable of satisfactorily discharging the duties of the office. "If you elect me GOVERNOR I promise to stop race track gambling in Charleston and run the blind tigers from Columbia and raise the banner of law observance," asserted Solicitor Cooper. He made a plea for greater development of our educational system, and supported the good roads movement.

 Harry Morrissey pleased the fans present with a clever rendition of that popular ballad entitled Playing the Game of Love.

New York. Nov. 10th, 1913.

Heart Songs came SATURDAY. The girls were
away, they didn't get in until Sunday afternoon.
I was up stairs writing some dull stuff for a maga-
zine when the old melodies floated up into
my den—I couldn't write any more, so I went down the parlor and by the grate.
We have not had such treating in years. The very
air blossomed with melody.
These songs took us in memory back to the old
farm, back to the double log house in the Southland,
sweet with the honeysuckle and the jasmine.
They took the battlefield and colored it with
glory and the crash of
musketry to music.

They told us the pathetic tale of the black man,
and the black nanny from all they loved, and
we felt humane and sympathetic.
They relighted the camp-fires of the revolution
along the valley of the Potomac where the bare-footed
Continentals wrested American liberty from British
tyrant and they increased reverence for the flag
of freedom.

They bore messages of love from mothers and
sweethearts, wandering boys, and brought back the
vows of ever true "to you, true."
They kindled the fires of the family hearth-
stone and their light shone back to the very cradle.

Heart Songs seem to sweep every string on the
harpsichord of human emotion.
One page would lead us gayly through fields of
flowers, the next would moisten eyes with
the dew of tears. Why this book was
called "Heart Songs."
The new Victrola with records from Caruso,
Garden and Tetrazzini has been put out of business.
We thank you for Heart Songs.

Respectfully yours,

EUGENE CHRISTIAN.

EAGLE PASS, Tex, April 1.—Despatches from the American consul at Durango forwarded to Washington via this city are reported today to announce that the federal Commander at Torreon has offered to surrender to General Villa, that a truce has been granted and that the federal and rebel commanders have met and are today arranging the terms of capitulation.

General Velasco, it is said, has called for a three hour armistice and offered to surrender the town if the garrison could march out with honors of war and if Villa would parole the officers and guarantee not to kill the volunteers as he has threatened. The despatch announcing the truce and offer of surrender has been forwarded to Washington.

William Blocker, American consul at Piedras Negras, refused to reveal the contents of the despatch from Durango but admitted that the message had been received and forwarded to Secretary Bryan. According to information from authentic sources, General Villa had taken the railroad station in Torreon and for the last two days has been working his way from house to house toward the center of the city. He is said to have taken nearly all the town but the assault resulted in an appalling loss of life on both sides. Last night General Velasco hoisted a white flag, it is said, and asked for three hours truce to present a proposition for surrender.

CHICAGO, Dec. 10—To the Editor of
The Bee About 4:00 p. m., November 17,
1914. John Rohrberg, while stealing a
ride on one of our freight trains at
Omaha, fell and was run over and so
badly injured that it was necessary to
amputate both his legs.

So many accidents of this kind are
constantly occurring, not only on the
tracks of this company, but in all parts
of the country, caused by persons walking on the tracks or tipping on the cars,
resulting in death or injury, that I have
been requested by the central safety
committee of this company to call your
attention to the matter.

You will find attached hereto a card
showing the statistics taken from the
reports of the Interstate Commerce Commission for twenty-four years ending
June 30, 1913, of accidents of this kind,
which show 10,000 persons killed and 11,251 persons injured walking on railroad
tracks and tipping on cars.

During the year ending June 30, 1913,
which is the last year for which we have
any records from the Interstate Commerce Commission, 5,555 persons were
killed while walking on the tracks or
tipping on the cars, and 6,510 injured,
nearly every injury being a permanent
disability.

This means that there were twenty
eight times as many trespassers killed
during that year as there were passengers
killed in train accidents during the same
year, over 100,000,000 passengers being
transported. Most of the trespassers
killed and injured are respectable citizens
or children and it seems to us that their
lives should be just as valuable to their
families and to the communities in which
they live as are the lives of passengers
who ride in the coaches.

Accidents of this kind, many of which
are especially deplorable, frequently
bringing poverty and destitution to the
families of the deceased, could easily be
prevented if laws were enacted penalizing
people trespassing on the tracks.

Thinking that possibly you or your
community may be interested in this
matter we call your attention to it.

F. A. RICHARDS
Chairman also of North Western
Central Safety Committee.

Another said, Christian missions are revolutionizing the world. Look at the vast amounts—fabulous sums contributed to send the gospel preacher and the Bible to the uttermost parts of the earth. Church conventions all over the country and the world reported thousands converted, and other thousands begging, like the man from Macedonia, for the gospel message.

Great Laymen's Missionary Movements held all over the country told us that with money enough the world would be evangelical and Christianized within a generation. The Hague Peace Conference was in session, doing its great work, to which the world looked for the accomplishment of great things. All over the world the cry of "peace, peace" was heard. All at once, with the suddenness of an earthquake, came the greatest war the world has ever known, mocking the churches and scattering theories hoary with age. Irony of fate! Not only war, but the worst, most brutal and barbarous and immense, springs up and out from the very midst. Cathedrals and churches shelled and burned, universities used as stables, colleges and seminaries closed, mission stations shattered, women and children beggared and pauperized. Hell turned loose among the people of the highest civilization on earth by professed Christian nations, each claiming that "heaven is on our side." And who can predict the end?

The Norfolk Virginian-Pilot, asks will the world "be deaf to the past and blind to the present," and we add "to the future?" The subject is too awful, too disappointing, too discouraging and too big to even think about calmly, much less write about. Hopes, plans, prospects have been shattered as paper doll house would be torn by hurricane. One hundred years from today, perhaps longer, the baneful results of this war will be seen and felt.

Man must rebuild its ruined structures of philosophy, sociology and theology but must wait the process of rebuilding until the devil has exhausted his strength and his resources, and given us room to build our scaffolds. A new civilization must be built and constructed totally unlike and different from this which has collapsed built upon different foundation. Preachers, and teachers of religions must construct new sermons and theses. The old ones seem not to have brought forth anything but war and devastation and destruction. Will we be "deaf to the past and blind to the future"? Like a pin-setter, we have been setting up and building up structures for the devil to knock down. We must build no longer upon the sand but upon The Rock. Won't we learn—won't Europe learn, that after all, the Christ of the Bible is the only great teacher, and the only great example? A civilization without Christ must inevitably collapse, however highly civilized we may become.

A "Christian Civilization" means a civilization permeated by the Spirit of the Christ. Nothing short of it deserves the name or will stand the test. "Marvel not that I said unto you, we must be born again," said the Great Teacher. And how many—for how few of us today, have any knowledge whatever of this "new birth"? Until sin and hell is exorcised from the hearts of men there can never be abiding peace among individuals or nations, and no amount or kind of human education or conduct will bring to a human being this "new birth."

The Record published last week an
account of negro, Andrew Johnson,
alas Joe Smith, whose real name is
johnson, having been arrested and
held in Jail here on suspicion of
stealing a horse. This suspicion has
proven to be correct in spite of the
long story told by the negro to the
contrary. 1t has developed that
Johnson borrowed a mule from a
man in Sumter county for the pur-
pose of going for a doctor. He
failed to return with the mule. and
several days later it was discovered
that he had traded it for a horse to
another negro man in near by
community. The owner of the mule
recovered his property, and then
the owner of the horse, with a party
of citizens, started in search of his
animal. Their search was futile
until late last week, when Sheriff
Graham was notified by the Sheriff
of Sumter that a horse had been
stolen in that county by a negro,
whose description he gave along
with that of the horse. A few days
ago the over of the horse, accom-
panied by an officer of Sumter, came
here for the thief and the stolen
horse. johnson was readily identi-
fed. The horse was in the custody
of Mr. j w King at Savage, in Flor
ence county, where johnson had
been arrested by Rural Policeman
Stancill. Sheriff Graham and the
Sumter men went to Mr. Kings place
and identified the horse, which an
swered in detail the owners descrip-
ton. Then it developed that johnson
had agreed to sell the horse to Mr.
King for $4,000, about half its
actual value, and on this poor pre-
text Mr. King refused to turn the
horse over to it's rightful owner
without the presentation of claim
and delivery papers. The owner
had to return to Sumter without
his horse.

The fall session of the Oskaloosa district conference of the Methodist Episcopal church was held at Bussey and proved a most helpful gathering. There were about forty present, for all or a part of the session. Rev. G. L. Minear, D. D., the new superintendent, presided and won the hearts of all the members by his deep interest in the work and his great brotherly love. H. G. Millice was reelected as secretary and treasurer.

The opening service of Monday evening included a great address on the "Battle of the Bottle in the November Election" by Rev. C. S. Cooper, district superintendent of the Anti-Saloon League. The reports of district superintendents and pastors indicated that the new year was starting out in good shape and gave good signs of advancement.

Inspiring and helpful sermons were preached by J. F. Robertson, of Knoxville; Frank E. Day, of Newton, and W. S. Gardner, of New Sharon. The closing address on Wednesday evening was by our own Miss Kate Ogborn, of New Sharon, but now of Wuhu, China, she having been in the mission field for the last twenty-three years.

John W. Roster, A. B. Richards and Wm. G. Barr, of Oskaloosa, and Roy N. Hillyar, of Pella, were licensed as local preachers and Arthur Hueser, of Kellogg, as an exhorter. The conference received greetings from Rev. C. L. Stafford, through Rev. Minear, to which the secretary, by instructions, responded.

A surprise awaited the conference when it was announced that Rev. W. A. Odell of Knoxville circuit, had been transferred to the Upper Iowa conference. The conference was favored with the presence of Rev. J. Meyers, treasurer of I. W. C. and Rev. C. S. Tenant, D. D., of Burlington district, who came to assist Pres. E. A. Schell, of I. W. C. in the educational campaign.

The work of the Iowa conference permanent fund was presented by G. L. Kendrick, and the Iowa Methodist Hospital by Rev. W. P. Stoddard.

A committee consisting of G. L. Minear, J. O. Kemble, T. C. Kennedy and J. A. Spyker was appointed to take under advisement the question of a tabernacle campaign for next year.

The topics discussed were full of interest and covered a variety of subjects, the entire session being greatly enjoyed by those present.

Barnes City was selected as the place for holding the next session.

The committee on resolutions submitted the following report:

Resolved—First, that we are grateful to the people of Bussey and their pastor, C. W. Cochran, for their kindness and hospitality in so royally entertaining us during the district conference.

Second, that we desire to express our appreciation of the special music rendered by the choir, the male quartet and the ladies' double quartet.

Third, that we appreciate the spirit with which our district superintendent, Rev. G. L. Minear, has entered upon the work of this district, and pledge him our loyal support.

Fourth, that we are pleased with the work of the committee in arranging such an excellent program, and for the continued service of our faithful secretary, Rev. H. C. Millice.

Fifth, that we have heard with pleasure the presentations of the claims of the Anti-Saloon League, Iowa Methodist Hospital and the permanent fund, and give our hearty endorsement of all these causes.

Sixth, that we are grateful to Bro. Robertson, Bro. Day, Bro. Gardner and Miss Kate Ogborn, of Wuhu, China, for their suggestive and helpful addresses, and to everyone who has helped to make this conference a success.

Seventh, that most of all we are thankful to God for His presence, which has made the addresses, discussions and fellowship of the sessions of this district conference an inspiration and help to everyone present.

A. N. Courtney,
T. X. Holiday,

using combination of sheer force

even though he took us home, he
couldn't get the "circus" out of our
systems, and in 1882 we started out in

him make his shows a success, and
he never turns anyone away for fear
In so doing he might be guilty of
an injustice to one of the innu-
merous abouts who for over 80 years
have helped make the name of Ring
known throughout the world.

ed on the part Of the public by

travelling public can get off and
on with some comfort; it often

in northern Wisconsin has just
been closed here whereby the Edward
Hines Lumber company disposes of all
its interests here to local people, who
are organizing a new corporation,
which will be headed by G. H. Werden,
for many years superintendent of the
Hines interests here.


The deal includes the sawmill, the
bank, the company store, the cutover
lands, which extend over many thousand
acres, and all the other interests
the Hines company had here. The
principal men in the new corporation
are Mr. Werden, Henry and Ole AK
Eess, who have been connected with the
State Bank of Mason, another
Hines concern, for many years, and
G. J. Larson, manager of the company
store.


The sawmill will be wrecked and
shipped away. It has been idle for
over a year, all of the Hines timber
tributary to this town having been
manufactured into lumber and long
since shipped away, but the lath mill
will be operated and custom sawing
will be done for the settlers. The store
and bank will continue in business,
but the new corporation will center
its efforts on securing new settlers
and opening up farms on its cutover
lands. The consideration has not been
announced, but it is stated that the
deal involves several hundred thousand
dollars.

Sporting Editor The Virginian.


Sir,—The stories in all the Richmond papers concerning the unpleasant incident between Manager Ryan and a spectator at Monday's game have been grossly one-sided, and have done serious injustice to the party of young men who were ejected from the grounds as the result of Manager Ryan's display of temper. While it is true the names of the party were not given, there were many in the grandstand who witnessed their embarrassment who did know them, and in simple justice their side of the case should be given.


The four young men in the party are respectable business men, who are liberal patrons of the game and know how to behave themselves in the grandstand. Monday one of them had good-naturedly chafed Ryan over his pitching changes, and at the time of the passed ball shouted something about the team needing a new catcher too. He used no insulting language at that or any other time. When he started over after the belligerent manager it was only after Ryan had hurled at him foul oaths which is sufficient provocation for any man to fight. Then the other members of the party, who had nothing whatever to do with the trouble and had not induced even the chatting, were ejected also, which goes to show the wisdom and forethought of the police. Manager Bradley, however, knew the men, sent a suit and promptly nipped the arrest proceedings in the bud.


There are plenty of witnesses who sat close around the party who can testify to these facts, including Ryan's foul language. You gentlemen of the press, I realize, were unable to see it fully from your position and could not hear any of it. The whole fault was Ryan's loss of temper over good-natured testing of a fan—jesting which is induced in every game and to which the players pay no attention. But Mr. Ryan, who is old enough to know better, had to play the baby act.


I can furnish you the names of as many witnesses as you want in proof of the statement that no language in the least calculated to insult Mr. Ryan was used by the spectator—not even after Mr. Ryan grossly insulted him.


I trust you can give space in your columns to this statement in view of the fact that only Mr. Ryan's side of it has appeared.


Yours truly,


SPECTATOR

London.—A dispatch to the Reuters Telegram Company from Paris quotes an official statement:

Owing to strategical considerations it has been impossible to cooperate earlier with the Belgian army in the defense of their country, but the agreements which we have undertaken are only the more solemn and our cooperation will be still closer and will be pursued with extreme energy.

We wish, indeed, to remain civilized and will do so till the end, despite this return to savagery on the part of a nation which has pretended to be an arbiter of civilization. But it is impossible to preserve toward our present adversaries the chivalrous generosity which until now has been the rule between soldiers.

Time for war with gloves on has passed. The enemies with whom we exchanged at Fontenoy courteous words before opening fire have become today our faithful and useful allies. We have before us unbridled savages. We owe to them only the strict observance of the rules of humanity and the laws of war.

The minister of war has issued strict instructions that German prisoners, officers as well as soldiers, are not to be treated with the consideration and favor which should be reserved for our own men. Life is as ours, naturally, but that is all we owe them.

But it was with a heavy heart that Miss Yorke took the train for Brookton, and with a heavier one that she reviewed John's sad little history. John wasn't John Ritchie, or John anything—just John. He was a wistful-eyed, brown-haired little fellow of six, with one shoulder much higher than the other, and a pronounced limp, whom the Children's Aid had rescued from a brutal father and a weak and helpless mother. They were not really his parents; he was a foundling. The woman had taken him in and tried to raise him in the face of her husband's anger and cruelty. But she herself had finally handed John over to the society,

And they had taken him, and given him food and shelter, and baths and clothing—everything, in fact, except love, which a society can hardly be expected to provide in large quantities.

And he was very hard to dispose of. No one wanted a child who was practically deformed, and who might never be able to go out in the world and do the work of men.

At last the Ritchies had come. They were a middle-aged couple, a farmer and his wife, living outside Brookton, whose two children lay in the little old Brookton graveyard. Ever since the first hurt of their own bereavement had softened, they had planned and dreamed of adopting a child. Now they had come, full of expectation, with the usual list of requirements: a fair, curly-haired boy four years old, healthy and of decent percentage.

But John's little limping, timid figure went straight to Henry Ritchie's heart.

"He's the one," Ellen, he had said. "We're going to take John home with us to be our little boy."

Ellen had been at first aghast, then dubious; but in the end she had been won over, and the two had carried John, bewildered and yet radiant, between them.

A new John developed in the sunshine of love and tenderness, a John who could laugh, and even sing, and who dug in the garden with his little spade just as if his back had been like every other boy's.

But now Mrs. Ritchie was dead, and John would have to come back to the shelter. The buggy drew up in front of the long white house, with its old side porch, and tears stood in Miss Yorke's eyes at the sight of the hanging crepe.

It was Henry Ritchie himself who answered her knock. A Henry Ritchie how changed from the well-preserved middle-aged man she had known. His suit of black hung shockingly about his lean figure; his eyes were tired and sunken.

"You came to see about John, I suppose?" he asked in a husky voice as soon as they were seated.

"Yes, Mr. Ritchie," answered Miss Yorke gently. "Miss Delmar wanted to know what your plans were."

"I'm going to keep right along living here. Can't John live with me?"

"I'm afraid not, Mr. Ritchie—no, unless you get a housekeeper to look after him."

"I can't get a housekeeper, no now," and Henry's voice trembled.

"Then I'm afraid we'll have to take him. I'm sorry—dreadfully sorry. But you can't alone take care of him, and our children have to be taken care of."

"I wish I could leave him with me." Yorke laid a comforting hand on his arm. "But those are my orders."

The man rose heavily. "All right," he said. "I'll dress him and pack his things and bring him down."

As soon as Miss Yorke saw John she realized that she must take him. He still wore the pretty clothes the Ritchies had bought him, but his hair should have been cut days before; there was a hole in one of his stockings—altogether he showed the lack of experienced care.

"Good afternoon, John," said Miss Yorke, brightly, but bit unsteadily. "Don't you want to go up to the car with me?"

"Yes, thank you," answered John, in his quaint, unchildish way. "And with Father."

That "father" cut the visitor to the heart. "No, father's not going," she managed to say. The man arose.

We quote for your information Section from the War Revenue Act No. 217, entitled "An Act to Increase the Internal Revenue and for other purposes."

"Express and freight: It shall be the duty of every railroad or steamboat company, carrier, express company or corporation or person whose occupation is to act as such, to issue to the shipper or consignor, or his agent, or person from whom any goods are &c. consigned for transportation, where charge exceeding 5 cents is made, a bill of lading, manifest, or other evidence of receipt and forwarding for each shipment received for carriage and transportation, whether in bulk or in boxes, bales, packages, bundles or not so enclosed or included; and such shipper, consignor, agent or person shall duly attach and cancel as is in this Act provided, to each of said bill of lading, manifests or other memorandum, a stamp of the value of 1 cent; Any failure to issue such bill of lading, manifest, or other memorandum as herein provided shall subject such railroad or steamboat company, carrier, express company, or corporation or person, to a penalty of $4,000 for each offense."

Under this act it is incumbent on the shipper to furnish the revenue stamps and affix such stamp to each dray receipt or bill of lading and cancel such stamp at time bill of lading or dray receipt is presented to the Agent of the carrier for signature.

In order to avoid delay, it is suggested that shippers provide themselves with supply of stamps to be affixed to all dray receipts or bills of lading, effective December 1st.

TRENTON, Nov. 18.—The argument in the attempt to keep Patrick Quinlan from serving his sentence of from two to seven years in the New Jersey state prison was heard by the Court of Errors and Appeals yesterday afternoon. Quinlan was convicted in Passaic county of melting violence. He was sentenced to state prison and an appeal was taken to the Supreme Court. A writ of habeas corpus was then sued out pending an appeal to the Court of Errors, and Quinlan is now at liberty.


He is one of the foremost members of the Industrial Workers of the World in this country, and with Big Bill Haywood, and others, was in charge of the I. W. W. strike of silk workers in Paterson last year. At a meeting of the strikers in the Turn Hall in Paterson, which was attended by about 1,400 persons, Quinlan is alleged to have made a speech, which in its tone was said to encourage and incite the persons assembled to assault, beat and do injury to a certain class of persons residing in Paterson. It was alleged in the indictment found against him that he uttered the following words: "I'll make a motion that we go to the silk mills, parade through the streets and club them out of the mills, drag them out of the mills, no matter how we get them out, we got to get them out."


Michael Dunn, prosecutor of the pleas of Passaic county, appeared for the unfolding of the indictment, and Henry Carless, Henry Marelli and Gustav Hunziker represented the I. W. W. leader before the court.


Tells of "ERRORS" in Record.


In behalf of Quinlan it was argued that there were specific errors in the record of the case to warrant the overturning of the conviction. The court was asked to examine the record of the case in the light of the recent industrial history of the state of New Jersey. Mr. John W. Thomas, for the first
time in the writer's knowledge, has
admitted that he would like to see
some other restriction upon trout
fishermen than our law prohibiting
the taking of fish under six inches in
length. The commissioner's admis-

$50 placed upon a resident of New

erman on a day's outing to bring

feature might meet with more gener-
al observance than the present

one predominating reason in favor of
the present six inch limit. The cul-
turists tell us that a five-inch trout

the process of helping to continue the
existence of the species.

remedy would not materially change
conditions. The best trout waters in
the state are here and the fishermen,
as a whole, are law-abiding. Partial-
ly due to the efforts of the Benning-

partially due to the arguments ad-
vanced by individuals, sentiment

ent law. Bennington county fisher-

brought about unless the trout that
are planted in the streams for stock-
ing purposes have chance to spawn.

Wallingford went back upstairs where he found Blackie holding a watch in his hand while Mr. Jackson drank the rainbow bender.

Wallingford, groaning with numbing drowsiness, dragged himself out of bed, dug his knuckles into his eyes, answered the telephone, wrangled in an attempt at suavity with a voice, slammed the receiver and leaned heavily against the telephone to gather up strength enough to lurch back to the most delicious spot in all the wide, wide world.

fourth Congress is organized in December,
1915, many familiar faces will be seen
in the two houses. At the same time,
some old favorites who were retired to

gone for the time, but yesterday's elec-

tariff Republican President. They are
convinced that Tuesday's election fur-
nishes ample proof that the nearly
100,000 Republicans who walked out

ilant, first, because they believe the Pro-

It Was, in Fact, a Case of "Turn About

Is Fair Play"

Sam Showalter was having a sale of his surplus stock. To start the sale he led out a milk cow, one of the best of his herd, and told the auctioneer she was four years old. John Dawson, a long, leathery, weather beaten fellow with a shrewd eye, bid in the cow. He gave Showalter check for the amount and said he would come for the cow the next day.

"I tell you, John," said Showalter when Dawson rode up the next morning to lead home his purchase, "I made a mistake yesterday. I said that cow was only four years old, but when I talked it over with the old woman last night I remembered that she is eight years old. It was another cow altogether that I had in mind.

"I didn't want to let a mistake like that go with a neighbor," continued Showalter, whose word was not usually accepted as entirely dependable in the community. "So I thought the fair thing to do was to tell you and just let you take your check back and I'll keep the cow."

Dawson squinted his eye approvingly at the cow—she had every mark of good milker—and then looked appraisingly at Showalter.

"Well, Sam," he said, "turn about is fair play. You made a mistake yesterday; I'll make one today and just keep the cow."—Youth's Companion.

Washington, July 15.—With all differences of opinion over proposed conservation legislation removed, passage of legislation on the subject at this session of Congress was today believed to be assured. The way was paved at a long conference at the White House last night.

President Wilson, members of the cabinet and of the House, spent several hours smoothing over differences of opinion over the Adamson general dam bill, now pending in the House, and the Ferris bill to regulate water power projects on public lands. As a result a complete agreement was reached between the authors of the two bills and when the conference broke up all parties predicted passage of the measures.

The disagreement over the two bills had delayed their consideration in the House. Consideration of the Adamson bill, it was announced today, will be continued as soon as the appropriation bills are out of the way. The conference decided to keep jurisdiction over all dams and water power sites on the public domain and those on property not in the public domain entirely separate. Minor changes were made in the Adamson bill in order that provisions thought to conflict with the Ferris bill might be made clearer and more definitely defined.

Those who participated in the conference in addition to the President: Democratic leaders, secretaries Garrison and Lane; Representative Adamson and Stevens, representing the Interstate and Foreign Commerce committee; and Representative Ferris and Lenroot, who represented the Public Lands committee.

Washington, November 1—Acting Secretary Lansing announced today the receipt of a message from American Consul Sprague at Gibraltar stating that prize court proceedings had begun in the case of the American steamship Kroonland, detained by British Authorities.

No reply has as yet been received from London to the formal protest made through Ambassador Page and the request for the release of the vessel. In the recent case of the steamer Brindilla, however, prize court proceedings actually had begun when the British government ordered the release of the vessel.

Consul Sprague reported that the Kroonland was discharging her cargo of 1400 tons of copper and 300 barrels of lubricating oil. The reason for this was not given. State department officials will await formal reply from London before making further representations. Inasmuch as copper and oil were placed on the contraband list after the Kroonland sailed, the American government probably will contend that the vessel has right to deliver her cargo. It is thought in some quarters, however, that the Kroonland may have discharged the copper and oil as a result of the offer of the British government to buy it.

While the consul's dispatch made no mention of the Kroonland's 1900 passengers, it is believed that if the vessel discharges her cargo for consideration by the prize court she may be allowed in the meantime to proceed to Italy and Greece with her neutral passengers. German and Austrian reservists, reported on board, would be taken off prisoners of war.

together, to which he added

more fuel, and soon a bright

light was cast about from the

blazing twigs. He then exam-

ined the ground infinitely, get-

ting down on hands and knees.

At this time we heard a slight

rustling in the brush to our

right as if coming from

some person or animal stealth-

ily creeping through the under-

growth. We looked back again

towards the fire. The Indian

was on his feet, pistol in hand.

"Down, boys!" I whispered,

loudly; and we dropped just in

time. Three reports from the

Indian's pistol awakened the

echoes from the mountain sides,

two bullets whistled past over

the log while the third "spat"

and embedded itself in the side

of the log opposite us. Three

more shots in rapid succession

followed, but he must have fired

the air, or up the hollow,

for we did not hear the bullets.

Knowing he had emptied his gun,

and believing it to be a signal to

the other Indians up the moun-

tain, I raised myself sufficiently

to see what his next move would

be. He was reloading his gun.

A single shot was heard away

up the mountain. He started in

that direction, and after a time

we heard his horse going rapidly

up the mountain and saw occa-

sional sparks fly from his shoes.

Not long after Indian and horse

had passed out of our zone of

sound we saw what at first we

thought to be a dog searching

the ground near the fire, but

after watching it for a time

agreed it was a wolf, and I then

suggested that we return to

the fire. We started around the

end of the log and away came

two or three other wolves that had been crouching in the

undergrowth within 80 yards of

us. We took turns at watching

for daylight, and during my

watch I saw several pairs of

eyes gleaming like tiny balls of

fire from the nearby thickets,

but not a sound was heard ex-

cept the snoring of my compan-

ions.

BY Alexander Hume Ford.

LONDON, Eng., June 15.—In London I visited the most perfectly equipped government tourist bureau of any I have seen, and it was that of British Columbia. It was on the second floor in Salisbury House, and it took me, a stranger, half day to find the place. I also visited on Cannon Street the tourist bureau of the Malay States, and the old offices of New South Wales, while other days were spent in seeking information bureaus of the other Australian and Pacific states; all of which accentuated the wisdom of Victoria, New South Wales and Tasmania combining and erecting the magnificent "Commonwealth building" in the most prominent location in London, just bordering on the great open area on which Earl Grey hopes to erect the Colonial building, and trust it will be completed as a Pan Pacific building. At present it would take two weeks to explore London and discover the different information bureaus of Pacific lands. Some of these are splendidly conducted, others are merely resting places for those who hold official jobs. In Melbourne House, for instance, among the forty or fifty men engaged in working for the Australian states, I doubt there is one over forty years of age, and the work they accomplish is certainly equal to that of all the other Pacific states in London combined. This is an age of youth and energy, especially in the tourist and immigration work.

In the British Columbia offices there are Mr. Turner and Mr. J. A. Turner, the one being the son of the other, the father acting as splendid advisory board, and on the son falls the effort of interesting those who come to inquire about British Columbia, and I know he does briskly and splendidly. He has hundreds of pamphlets from every part of British Columbia tastefully displayed, and he knows where each one is to be found. In ten seconds he will have as many pamphlets in your hand, and then begin to tell you with whom you may communicate in each district of British Columbia for further information. Moreover, there is an excellent library of British Columbia magazines and newspapers. There is an atmosphere of British Columbia about the place, and you begin to realize that this section of the world must be a pretty live, go-ahead sort of proposition. The young clerks about the place are energetic and enthusiastic, and moreover, they are intelligent. Evidently British Columbia has appointed them to be of use and not as ornaments or in payment for some political debt to their fathers.

Possibilities for Hawaii.

I am paying very little attention in Europe, or elsewhere, or to anything not closely connected with promotion matters, and realize now, more than ever, the wonderful possibilities for Hawaii when she takes up the advanced methods being rapidly adopted by the most progressive countries, not only of the Pacific, but of Europe. It was therefore with some delight that I read a communication just received from Burton Holmes, in which he informs me that he shall visit Pacific lands, including Hawaii, New Zealand and Australia, in the summer of 1915, and make these countries the subjects of his lectures during the following season which is the winter following the San Francisco Exposition, and now is the time for us to play up these lectures and reach out for the round-the-Pacific tourist, not only from America but from Europe, for very low rates are promised from European ports by Suez and by rail across Siberia to those who will join the round-the-Pacific cruises.

In a few days I shall be in New York, and my first visit will be to the Pan-American building, one of the new skyscrapers that I understand has been built in the great New World metropolis as the home of the commercial museums of the Latin American countries, for I have by no means lost hope that we shall yet have a Pan-Pacific building in New York City where every tourist bureau of the Pacific, every immigration bureau, and all of the transportation companies of the Great Ocean will have their American headquarters; from whence in America the attractions of Pacific lands to the tourist, immigrant and investor will be sent broadcast. Already Japan has her official tourist bureau and commercial museum in New York City, and is as ready to unite with other Pacific countries in a plan to have Pan Pacific building as are Australia and the Philippines, while the tea people of Java will make a desperate effort to have the Dutch East Indies embark in the venture.

Resolved by the assembly, the senate concurring. That the foregoing proposed amendment to the constitution of the state of Wisconsin be, and the same is hereby agreed to by this legislature.

Vernecoe fort war, ging der Maler wieder an seine Arbeit. So macht es noch mehr zu Wuthe auf: sein, als die Sorge aus der Rheine gekommen war.

Vernecoe feierte aus in sein eigenes Studio. Er putzte die Stiefel, putzte sein Haar mit Pomade Elm und zog den besseren Rock an, den er seit zwei Wochen nicht mehr getragen hatte. Dann setzte er seinen Hut auf, nahm den Regenschirm unter den Arm und machte sich daran, den Auftrag auszuführen, den er mit allen Einzelheiten in seinem Gedankenkopf umherging. In ihm war alles in Ordnung. Heute wollte er noch einmal in "Bunten Bruno" einen Drink tun.

Der Chef des Sanatoriums Sato, mit einem Schützling im Arm, eine Frau, die der teilnehmenden Mitglieder ihre dankbaren Zeugen in Vertrauen. Vernecoe, der auf seinem Fahrrad war, gab sofort einen Lauf zum besten, wie man kleine Fehler auflösen und einen Mann behandeln müsse.

Mit arbeitsamem Geist und starkem Lust auf Leben verließ er eine kleine Stube beim "Bunten Bruno." Statt draußen in den beiden Omnibusse aufsteigen, fand er es viel angenehmer in der stillen Stube des kleinen Wirtshauses, und es war fast fünf Uhr, als er in der unterschiedlichen Stimmung nach dem "Anger" ins Freie trat und in den Omnibus nach Kammeritz stieg. Dort wanderte er in den Straßen umher und fragte jedermann nach der Abendzeit; gegen elf Uhr hielt er eine politische Rede im Sanatorium der "Meistersonne"; aber ob er sie in Paris, Berlin, Wien oder Madrid befand, das hatte er nicht wissen können; es war ihm allzu gleichgültig.

Sobald Vernecoe aus dem Atelier gelaufen war, setzte er zusehends wieder an seine Arbeit. Es war nun doch etwas geschehen und das Warten kam ihm entgegen. Von dem, den er begleiten sollte, auf der Fahrt, war er mit dem Ende der Reise fast schon am Ende, nachdem er ihr die Tür: Der Rhein geöffnet hatte. Doch, Vernecoe ahnte es nicht, daß Vernecoe eigentlich "der gute Geist des guten Glückes" habe, während er mit allem Gier an einem Bilde matte und bei erschöpften Leuten wie Elm schlummerte. Er wartete ihm gerade in seine Stimmung. Luft und Arm auswendig.

Plötzlich hielt er inne, sprang auf und stand mit der Palette in der Hand, mit der Pfeife in der anderen Hand da. Schritte lieber ihm, angenehm – Elm wusste, dass es auf dem großen Platz leben – ein Zweifel, die er nicht hatte.

Die Tür ging auf – und seine Kunst war nun vor ihm.

Seit dem Tage, an dem er Mann im Wirtshaus gesehen war, hatte sich Fräulein Sande fortgehend in Gedanken mit der Frage beschäftigt, ob er in aller Welt neugeschehen etwas an der Geschichte wusste? Hatte er seine gebildete Anmutung auf den Anteil und ein Moment vertraut auf Sinn gehabt oder handelte es sich um eine andere? HALIFAX, N. S., May 18.—Snatched from the very jaws of death after thirteen days of famine on an Arctic sea, four survivors of a crew of fifteen who escaped a fiery fate when the freight steamer Columbian burned May 3, arrived here today on the United States revenue cutter Seneca, which picked them up after eleven of their number starved.


Officer Robert Tierney, sailors Oscar Sendal and Peter Belanger and Fireman Mitchell Ludwigsen, were the four who arrived today aboard the Seneca. Stripped of their clothes by their famishing mates, the bodies of the eleven other sailors, one by one, were consigned to the pitiless sea. Each went overboard after the spark of life had fled.


Word by word, after their rescue, the starving men told in gasps of their awful experience. Water and biscuit gone, they said, the creatures existed on scraps of bark, catching in tarpaulins and in the jackets of their dead fellows the rain which fell from the limitless sky bending above the great gray waste of water on which their boat floated.


When the Columbian, of the Ley Line Inc., burned at sea, 50 miles south of Sable Island, three boats full of her crew left the flaming vessel. Sifted in the wallow of the waves, they separated. Two days later, two of the boats, containing part of the crew, were picked up by the liners Franconia and Manhattan. The third, on which the Seneca rescued, was thought to be lost.


The revenue cutter was on duty as an ice patrol-boat, scanning the sea for icebergs, when on Sunday morning the lookout shouted, "Boat ahead!"


The starboard bow. In an instant Captain Johnston ordered full steam ahead and eager eyes watched the little derelict as the cutter prowled through the waves. No sign was to be seen from the decks of the ship, but to make sure, the captain ordered the gig overboard for closer examination.


When their boathook gripped the gunwale of the drifting lifeboat, four men huddled together in her bottom were found. All were in a state of absolute collapse. They could not speak. Their lack-lustre eyes and hollow cheeks plainly told their story of starvation. The pile of clothing on which they crouched was the first indication that others who shared their fate had gone to the bottom of the sea. Spoonfuls of brandy and sips of water were given the rescued four immediately. Then wrapped in blankets, they were laid anew in the bottom of the boat and the gig was pulled back to the Seneca with the lifeboat in tow. In slings the rescued men were hoisted up the cutter's side. Her physician ministered to them and from very exhaustion, they slept.


When the cutter's nose was turned toward Halifax and all speed made for this port.


After several hours rest in the sick bay of the Seneca, and when judiciously administered food had stilled their hunger pangs, the rescued men told briefly the story of their ordeal. Weakly they gasped on how, when the Columbian burned, their boat was third to leave the side. österreichischen Botschaft, „und die
österreichische Regierung will für alle
nach der Agitation gegen die Integrität
der österreichischen Lande ein
Ende bereiten und diese Agitation hat
ihren Ursprung in Serbien. Ob dies
vor der Regierung fortgeführt
wird oder nicht, ist absolut gleichgültig,
daß diese Agitation
die Verantwortung für die Krise
so bald in Sarajevo trägt.

Österreich will nicht
nachgeben, aber die Situation muss unter allen
Umständen erklärt werden. Serbien
gegenüber mußte man ihm etwas
schärferes Sprache bieten, als es
einem anderen Staat aussetzte, wo
unsere Güter bestehen. Die beiden
Staaten sind für Österreich
von der allerhöchsten Wichtigkeit. Das
eine jedoch für die anderen Mächte
keinerlei Bedeutung. Die anderen
Mächte haben in ihrem eigenen
Interesse handelt, indem sie auf einer
Neutralisierung des Streits bestehen.
Es ist zu plädieren und zu hoffen,
daß Europa im Allgemeinen zu der
Einigkeit kommt, daß Österreich eins
und allein seine Rechte behauptet.“

„Russland wird alles in einer
Nacht unternehmen, um ein
friedliches Verhältnis zwischen
Österreich und Serbien herbeizuführen.“ So äußerte sich am Sonntag
ein Vertreter der russischen Botschaft.
Im Laufe des Abends eine Reihe
von Konferenzen zwischen dem russischen
Botschafter Graf Gendrosnoff
und Vertretern der französischen Botschaft
stattgefunden.

„Wir müssen fristlos „Dienst haben“, und der bestehende Zustand fort, hat Russland in Wien als
eines der Anzeichen der Streit nachgesucht, welche für die Unterbrechung der Antwort auf das Ultimatum festgesetzt
wurde. Man Russland in der Seitenstellung, daß wenn nur die
notwendige Zeit auszusetzen wird, eine fristlose Lösung gefunden werden kann. Serbien würde Russland die
Verantwortung Österreichs zu unterstützen
beipflichten, für welche es die Be-
weisung besitzen ließen, und für alle
DIE Serbien genügsam zu sein
im Stande wäre.

Die Abmachungen der österreichischen
Seite sind jedoch bereit, daß sie vielleicht
eine ruhige Lösung der Ankunft
kommen ist, daß russische Intervention
geschlossen ist und daß
nicht mehr als die einfache Gesetzes
unterstützung mit Serbien hinter der Grenze steht. Ferner könnte Russland
nicht gleichgültig und untätig mit tun,
wenn die Stellung Serbiens in
Europa in Gefahr geraten ist. Russ-
land sieht sich durch die Hoffnung
an, daß dies ein Ende lassen wird, um diese Kontroverse ohne Ausbruch des europäischen Krieges
beizulegen.“

Sarajevo, 26. Juli.

zeitungen fordern unmitelbar Sir Go.

In order to make this loan as small as possible I suggest that the expenditures in every department be reduced to a minimum until the taxes for this year become available and that the collectors for the years previous to 1914 be required to complete their collections and make full settlement with the city treasurer within such time as the city council may order." In this connection it would seem that the city council for its own protection should secure the services of a chartered accountant who after a thorough examination should furnish a statement showing the exact condition of the city finances and property. The city treasurer's report, which had always been published before the annual election until the advent of the late mayor, has since that time been withheld until midsummer, and all that is known at this time concerning the city finances is that the appropriations for the past year have been overdrawn to an aggregate of many thousand dollars. The present city government owes it to itself, and to the community as well, to take account of stock now, and thus avoid possible misrepresentation in the future.

Ninguna de estas personas recibió lastimaduras. La Sta. Walsh vino el Domingo juntamente con otros miembros del coro de la iglesia de la Immaculate Conception en un viaje dado por el pastor de la iglesia, el Rev. A. M. Mandari, S. J.

Stanton, de esta ciudad, y ahora perteneciente a Walter Weiman, de Albuquerque, se soltó fuera del poder de manejo y cayó sobre la pared en la cumbre de la Cuesta de la Bajada. JUNEAU, Feb. 3.—The attorneys for the Pacific Coast Steamship Co., the Alaska Steamship Co., the Northern Pacific Wharves Co., the White Pass and Yukon Railroad and the Canadian Steamship line today pled guilty to the indictments brought against the several companies because of rebates given to the favored shippers, and because of the combination in restraint of trade, which is in violation of the Sherman antitrust act.

Judge Robert W. Jennings fined the Pacific Coast company $6,250, the Alaska Steamship Company $5,000, the North Pacific Wharves and Trading Company $10,000, the White Pass and Yukon railroad $2,000, the Canadian Steamship Company $3,500.

The fines were imposed after Judge Jennings had received instructions from Attorney General McReynolds to accept the plea of guilty.

The cases have hung fire for two years and involved nearly all of the transportation companies of South-eastern Alaska. The Humboldt steamboat, operated as an independent boat, claimed that it was being discriminated against by the different dock owners and that shippers were given low rate in order to keep them from shipping with the Humboldt so that in a few months the boat could be driven off the run.

Washington, July 22.—The department of agriculture has discovered that certain oranges are being shipped under false descriptions in the bills of lading or invoices as to their variety. The department has examined some of these shipments and has found out that while these oranges are being sold to consignees as being a better variety than they are, the actual boxes of oranges are either not labeled at all or are not labeled in accordance with the variety mentioned in the records of sale. Some of these oranges are represented, for example, as being Valencias and examination shows them to be another variety.

The matter is being carefully investigated with a view to determine the rights of the department under the Food and Drugs Act to take action against such shipments. In the meantime, jobbers and others are advised to examine oranges packed in boxes either unlabeled or without any distinctive variety designation, in order to satisfy themselves whether these oranges are as represented by the producer or shipper.

Similarly, retail purchasers who are in the habit of buying oranges according to variety should assure themselves that the oranges are as represented by the dealer.

In travelling over the plains of western Texas, writes contributor, I have now and then come on two little isolated heaps of rock that at first glance seemed not at all remarkable. After a time, I noticed that one heap was generally about three feet high, and the other about a foot lower. The two were always within a few feet of each other, and usually on an elevation of plateau that had view of the country for five miles or more.


The rocks were roughly heaped together, as if left by children at play; I sometimes wondered if they could be the ruins of an ancient stone building; but that was improbable, for there was scarcely another stone in sight. Years later I learned the actual significance of these rock heaps from an old Indian whose mind was stored with all the legends and customs and deeds of his people. According to him, when the Great Spirit tapped up the mighty rivers of the plains, he left springs and water basins here and there for the antelope and the Indian. These the antelope easily found by scent, but the Indian had to search long and anxiously for them. Once found, they were seldom lost—thanks to these rude rock heaps.


I watched the old fellow crouch down behind the taller heap, sight over the low one, and mark the farthest object in straight line, which in this case was a clump of bushes on the horizon. Washington, D. C., March 6.

The Sims bill to repeal the Panama tolls exemption was favorably reported by the house commerce committee today by a vote of seventeen to four. Representatives Doremus and O'Shaughnessy of Michigan, Democrats, Knowland of California, Republican, and Lafferty of Washington, Progressive, opposed it.

The bill as reported by the committee is brief and to the point. It simply provides that the sentence in the Panama Canal Act reading:

NO tolls shall be levied on vessels engaged in the coastwise trade of the United States shall be repealed.

Members who voted against it pointed out that another provision relating to minimum tolls also must be repealed or the whole question still will be open and the United States may in discretion allow American vessels free use of the canal.

Chairman Adamson immediately began work on a report to the house and declared he would press the repeal just as rapidly as possible. The committee also voted to ask for a special rule to expedite the repeal. With three days allowed for the minority report, it is probable no effort will be made to take up the bill in the house before next Thursday.

At the White House there was every evidence that the administration was pushing for action.

The independent association, during a long session behind closed doors, elected officers for the ensuing year; listened to various reports from the clubs composing the circuit and then adjourned with the announcement that the meeting would be continued tomorrow morning.

As if to impress the older leagues with stay, James A. Gilmore was reelected president for term of five years.

In addition he was selected to serve as treasurer for a similar period. Robert B. Ward, president of the Brooklyn Federals, was elected vice president and Lloyd Rieckert secretary, each for a term of one year.

An Want to Stick.

President Gilmore stated that the reports of all the clubs as read at the meeting showed that the league was in a satisfactory financial condition, and that the sentiment of the club owners was unanimously in favor of continuing the organization along the lines originally laid out a year ago. He denied that any initiative had been taken by the Federals looking toward peace with the National and American leagues, or that changes in the present circuit had been discussed at the meeting.

Gilmore added that there was no truth in the reports that the Ward brothers of this city were negotiating for the purchase of the New York Americans, or that Charles Weeghman was about to buy controlling interest in the Chicago Nationals. Harmony and satisfaction with the 1914 season and the prospects for next year were the keynotes of the meeting, it was said.

Ring of Defiance.
There was a ring of defiance in the talk of various officers and club owners of the league. President Gilmore said no overtures toward peace had been suggested at the meeting, either by the Federals or the old leagues. Twelve players, who finished the season with organized base ball, have signed Federal league contracts for 1915, and six or eight more are expected to enter the new league within a short time, according to Gilmore. He said that the league had failed to secure Tesreau, Burns and Fletcher of the New York Nationals, as had been hoped, because each was bound by a three-year contract.

Although the Federal league magnates refused to discuss various reports regarding the future plans of the individual clubs of the league, there were several rumors which were given credence by those who followed the meeting in an unofficial capacity.

New York May Get Club.
Chief of these was a report that the Wards would place a Federal club on Manhattan island in case organized base ball refused to recognize the belligerents. Another was that a re-arrangement of the circuit would be made, eliminating several of the long jumps and unprofitable cities now included in the organization.

Weeghman denied that he had discussed the purchase of the Chicago Nationals in Cincinnati before coming to this city for the annual meeting. He said his talk with Hermann was regarding the disposition of the third club in Chicago, in case a settlement of the difficulties between the old and new leagues was reported.

In spite of all, Aunt Mary awoke and had to tell her the news, also, that Dick was not at home.

"Don't you want me to go with you, Margie?"

As we entered the hall the telephone rang. I answered and Jim Edie's voice asked, "Is this Margie?"

"Yes, Jim."

"I found Dick, Margie, and he'll be over in about an hour. Is his father still alive?"

"I don't know, Jim. Just got here myself. Tell Dick to come to the phone."

There was a short silence and then Jim said: "He can't come, Margie, but he's racing up so that he can get there as soon as possible." My heart almost stopped beating. clews.

girl's body but, like other efforts, that

culated. While at Atlantic City Griscom

and declared IT would go down in history

amount was expended by newspapers,

by the police. From time to time there
have been rumors that Dorothy had re-
turned, but these have always been de-
manded at the Arnold home.
